questions.stem: The peripheral nervous system divides into which two systems?
questions.why: The PNS divides into the somatic nervous system, controlling voluntary muscles, and the visceral or autonomic nervous system, which further divides into sympathetic and parasympathetic.

options.t: Sensory and motor divisions
options.why: Those describe fiber direction, not system divisions.

options.t: Sympathetic and parasympathetic
options.why: Those are subdivisions of the autonomic system.

options.t: Somatic and visceral (autonomic)
Central and peripheral divisions
options.why: Central is not part of the peripheral system.

questions.stem: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there, and what do they carry?
questions.why: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves positioned bilaterally, receiving sensory and motor messages to and from the central nervous system.

options.t: 24 pairs, carrying sensory and motor traffic
options.why: That overstates the number of pairs.

options.t: 12 pairs, carrying sensory traffic only
options.why: Twelve pairs are the cranial nerves.

options.t: 31 pairs, carrying motor traffic only
options.why: Spinal nerves carry sensory traffic as well.

options.t: 31 pairs, carrying sensory and motor traffic

questions.stem: What is a nerve plexus and what advantage does it provide?
questions.why: Spinal nerves combine in five areas of the body to form networks where the roots come together and transmit their impulses through a common nerve. That arrangement lets several spinal nerves control one area — built-in redundancy.

options.t: A cluster of nerve cell bodies outside the cord
options.why: That describes a ganglion.

options.t: A junction between a nerve and a muscle fiber
options.why: That describes a neuromuscular junction.

options.t: A bundle of fibers that speeds up conduction
options.why: Speed comes from myelination, not plexus formation.

options.t: A network serving one area from many roots

questions.stem: In how many areas of the body do spinal nerves combine to form plexuses?
questions.why: The spinal nerves combine in five areas to form the five main plexuses — cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal regions.

options.t: Twelve
options.why: Twelve is the thoracic nerve count.

options.t: Five
Three
options.why: That undercounts the plexus regions.

options.t: Eight
options.why: Eight is the cervical nerve count, not the plexus count.

questions.stem: Where do the cranial nerves arise, and how many pairs exit from the brainstem?
questions.why: Twelve pairs of cranial nerves arise from the base of the brain, and all but two pairs exit from the brainstem.

options.t: Twelve pairs, most leaving the brainstem
Twelve pairs, all leaving the spinal cord
options.why: Cranial nerves arise from the brain, not the cord.

options.t: Twelve pairs, most leaving the spinal cord
options.why: They exit from the brainstem, not the cord.

options.t: Thirty-one pairs, all from the brainstem
options.why: Thirty-one pairs are the spinal nerves.

questions.stem: Cranial nerves may carry which types of fibers?
questions.why: Cranial nerves may carry sensory fibers, motor fibers, or a combination of sensory and motor fibers — which is why testing them can assess either or both functions.

options.t: Autonomic fibers only
options.why: Autonomic fibers travel with some but not all.

options.t: Sensory, motor, or both
Sensory fibers only
options.why: Some cranial nerves carry motor fibers too.

options.t: Motor fibers only
options.why: Some cranial nerves carry sensory fibers too.

questions.stem: The autonomic nervous system is best described as which of the following?
questions.why: The autonomic nervous system is the part of the PNS not under voluntary control. Its two divisions are the sympathetic — fight or flight — and the parasympathetic — rest and digest.

options.t: The sensory portion of the CNS
options.why: Sensory input is separate from autonomic control.

options.t: The involuntary part of the PNS
The reflex portion of the CNS
options.why: Reflexes involve the cord but the ANS is peripheral.

options.t: The voluntary portion of the PNS
options.why: That describes the somatic nervous system.

questions.stem: Once the PNS collects information and it is processed into an action potential, what are the three possible outcomes?
questions.why: The PNS collects and relays information about the body and external environment through stimuli. Messages processed into action potentials are brought to conscious thought for filtration, generate an automatic response (a reflex), or are discarded as unimportant.

options.t: Conscious thought, reflex, or discarded
Stored as memory or else discarded
options.why: Memory storage is not one of the three outcomes listed.

options.t: Converted to a hormonal signal
options.why: Nervous signals stay electrochemical rather than hormonal.

options.t: Conscious thought only, then acted upon
options.why: Some signals produce a reflex without reaching consciousness.

questions.stem: What are the general senses?
questions.why: General senses are how the body gathers information from its environment. Pain, temperature, touch, pressure, and position are monitored throughout the body by receptors in different tissues.

options.t: Sensations arising from the skin only
options.why: General senses come from many tissues, not skin alone.

options.t: Reflexes controlling internal organs
options.why: Those are autonomic reflexes rather than senses.

options.t: The five named special sense organs
options.why: Those are the special senses, not the general ones.

options.t: How the body reads its environment

questions.stem: What is the difference between somatic and visceral sensory information?
questions.why: Somatic sensory information covers the body and the environment. Visceral sensory information supplies data about the internal organs.

options.t: Somatic uses cranial nerves; visceral spinal
options.why: Both types travel by spinal and cranial routes.

options.t: Somatic covers the body; visceral the organs
Somatic covers the organs; visceral the body
options.why: The two are reversed here.

options.t: Somatic is voluntary; visceral is under autonomic control
options.why: Voluntary and autonomic describe motor output. The somatic/visceral split here is about where the sensory information comes from.

questions.stem: Pain receptors are called nociceptors. What are they sensitive to?
questions.why: Nociceptors are sensitive to mechanical, thermal, electrical, or chemical stimuli that could damage the body — a broad set of triggers, all signaling potential harm.

options.t: Mechanical, thermal, or chemical harm
Mechanical pressure and stretch only
options.why: Nociceptors also respond to heat and chemicals.

options.t: Chemicals from injured cells only
options.why: Mechanical and thermal stimuli count as well.

options.t: Joint position and muscle length
options.why: That describes proprioceptors.

questions.stem: How do visceral and somatic pain differ in character?
questions.why: Visceral pain is deep, internal, enclosed within a cavity — chest, abdomen, pelvis. Somatic pain is in superficial tissues like skin, bones, muscles, and joints, and is generally MORE intense and MORE precisely localized than visceral pain.

options.t: Visceral is superficial; somatic is deep
options.why: Visceral pain is the deep, internal type.

options.t: Somatic is sharper and better localized
Both are equally sharp and localized
options.why: They differ markedly in both qualities.

options.t: Visceral is sharper and better localized
options.why: Somatic pain is the sharper, better localized type.

questions.stem: What is referred pain?
questions.why: Referred pain is perceived somewhere other than its true source and occurs frequently with GI disorders — which is why cardiac pain can present in the jaw or arm.

options.t: Pain caused by peripheral nerve damage
options.why: Nerve damage may cause phantom rather than referred pain.

options.t: Pain felt away from its true source
Pain persisting after healing is complete
options.why: Persistence after healing is chronic pain.

options.t: Pain felt in an absent body part
options.why: That describes phantom pain.

questions.stem: What is phantom pain, and what may cause it?
questions.why: Phantom pain is the sensation of pain in a body part that is no longer present — the classic example being after limb amputation. It may occur secondary to damage to a peripheral nerve.

options.t: Pain referred from an organ to the skin
options.why: That describes referred pain.

options.t: Pain in a limb that is no longer present
Pain arising within the CNS rather than PNS
options.why: It arises from peripheral nerve damage.

options.t: Pain with no identifiable physical cause
options.why: Phantom pain has a clear cause in the missing limb.

questions.stem: What is notable about how pain and temperature sensations are conveyed?
questions.why: Thermoreceptors are nerve endings that respond to heat, and sensations of pain and temperature are conveyed by the same type of receptor.

options.t: They are conveyed by the same type of receptor
They travel along entirely separate nerve tracts
options.why: They share the same receptor type.

options.t: Temperature reaches consciousness but pain does not
options.why: Both reach conscious awareness.

options.t: Temperature is conveyed by mechanoreceptors and pain by thermoreceptors
options.why: Thermoreceptors handle temperature, not mechanoreceptors.

questions.stem: Mechanoreceptors, also called tactile receptors, monitor for what?
questions.why: Mechanoreceptors (tactile receptors) monitor changes in physical properties. Tactile receptors in the skin are sensitive to light touch, while others are stimulated by heavy pressure.

options.t: Joint position within space
options.why: Proprioceptors handle position.

options.t: Tissue and blood temperature
options.why: Thermoreceptors handle temperature.

options.t: Blood chemical composition
options.why: Chemoreceptors handle blood chemistry.

options.t: Physical change such as touch

questions.stem: Where are proprioceptors found and what do they do?
questions.why: Proprioceptors track position in space and are found in joints, skeletal muscles, and tendons. Baroreceptors measure pressure changes and chemoreceptors measure chemicals in the body or bloodstream.

options.t: Bloodstream, measuring chemical levels
options.why: Chemoreceptors measure chemical levels.

options.t: Joints and muscles, tracking position
Carotid arteries, measuring pressure
options.why: Baroreceptors measure pressure there.

options.t: Skin surface, detecting light touch
options.why: Tactile receptors sit in the skin.

questions.stem: Which receptor type measures changes in pressure?
questions.why: Baroreceptors measure changes in pressure. Chemoreceptors measure chemicals in the body or bloodstream, and proprioceptors track position.

options.t: Baroreceptors
Thermoreceptors
options.why: Those respond to heat.

options.t: Chemoreceptors
options.why: Those measure chemicals in the body or blood.

options.t: Proprioceptors
options.why: Those track position in space.

questions.stem: Where are the olfactory receptors located, and what do they respond to?
questions.why: The upper nasal cavity contains olfactory receptors, and olfactory cells respond to chemicals dissolved in the mucus.

options.t: Upper nasal cavity, sensing dissolved odors
Oropharynx, sensing chemicals in the saliva
options.why: Taste, not smell, uses the oral route.

options.t: Frontal sinus, sensing changes in pressure
options.why: The sinuses hold no olfactory receptors.

options.t: Lower nasal cavity, sensing dry particles
options.why: The receptors sit in the upper cavity and need dissolved chemicals.

questions.stem: Trace the sequence by which a smell becomes a perceived odor.
questions.why: After the chemicals reach a threshold level they bind with proteins in the olfactory receptors, causing a change in membrane permeability that creates an action potential. Those impulses travel through the olfactory nerves to olfactory centers in the brain, which interpret them as odors.

options.t: Bind the olfactory nerve directly, then fire
options.why: The chemicals bind receptor proteins first.

options.t: Bind receptor proteins, alter permeability, fire
Dissolve in blood for central chemoreceptors
options.why: Odorants dissolve in mucus, not blood.

options.t: Stimulate mechanoreceptors that signal the brain
options.why: Smell uses chemoreception, not mechanoreception.

questions.stem: Taste receptors respond to which four primary taste sensations?
questions.why: The taste buds in the mouth allow the sense of taste, and taste receptors respond to four primary sensations: sweet, salty, sour, and bitter.

options.t: Sweet, salty, sour, and bitter
Sweet, salty, sour, and umami
options.why: Umami is not among the four listed.

options.t: Sweet, bitter, spicy, and sour
options.why: Spicy is a pain sensation rather than a taste.

options.t: Salty, sour, bitter, and metallic
options.why: Metallic is not one of the four primaries.

questions.stem: The sense of sight is driven by which structures?
questions.why: Sight is driven by the eyes, their accessory structures, the optic nerve, and the tracts that connect it to the brain.

options.t: The globe, lens, and cornea only
options.why: The neural component is missing here.

options.t: Eyes and the oculomotor nerve alone
options.why: The optic nerve carries the visual signal.

options.t: The retina and visual cortex only
options.why: The optical structures are needed as well.

options.t: Eyes, optic nerve, and their tracts

questions.stem: The eye has two major components. What are they?
questions.why: The optical part gathers and focuses light to form an image; the neural part — the retina — converts that optical image into a neural code the brain can process.

options.t: A refracting part and a protective part
options.why: Protection is not one of the two major components.

options.t: A muscular part and an optical part
options.why: Muscle movement is an accessory function.

options.t: An optical part and a neural part
A lens for focus and a nerve for transmission
options.why: This omits the retina's coding role.

questions.stem: Which two aspects of light does the eye distinguish?
questions.why: The eye distinguishes brightness, also called luminance, and wavelength, which is color.

options.t: Intensity and direction
options.why: Direction is judged by the brain, not the eye's two aspects.

options.t: Wavelength and velocity
options.why: Light velocity is not distinguished by the eye.

options.t: Brightness and wavelength
Contrast and saturation
options.why: Those are derived qualities, not the two named.

questions.stem: How is an image brought into focus, and what is the nature of the image landing on the retina?
questions.why: Focus comes from altering the shape and thickness of the lens. The image focused on the retina is an upside-down, miniature version of the environment in front of the eye — the brain does the reorienting.

options.t: Eye muscles contract; image is life-size
options.why: The image is miniature, not life-size.

options.t: Retina shifts position; image lands upright
options.why: The retina stays fixed; the lens changes shape.

options.t: Pupil size changes; image is mirrored
options.why: Pupil size controls light entry, not focus.

options.t: Lens shape changes; image lands inverted

questions.stem: The organs of hearing are divided into which three portions?
questions.why: The organs of hearing divide into external, middle, and inner ear. The external and middle ear are involved in hearing only; the inner ear functions in both hearing and balance.

options.t: Pinna, canal, and cochlea
options.why: Those are all parts of the external and inner ear.

options.t: External, middle, and inner ear
Outer, tympanic, and cochlear
options.why: Tympanic and cochlear are structures within those portions.

options.t: External, membranous, and vestibular
options.why: Membranous and vestibular are inner ear components.

questions.stem: Which portion of the ear functions in both hearing and balance, and which cranial nerve controls it?
questions.why: The inner ear functions in both hearing and balance, controlled by cranial nerve VIII — the vestibulocochlear nerve.

options.t: The external ear, controlled by cranial nerve VIII
options.why: The external ear serves hearing only.

options.t: The inner ear, controlled by cranial nerve VIII
The middle ear, controlled by cranial nerve VII
options.why: The middle ear serves hearing only.

options.t: The inner ear, controlled by cranial nerve V
options.why: Cranial nerve V is the trigeminal, not the auditory nerve.

questions.stem: What is the function of the eustachian tube in hearing?
questions.why: The eustachian tube is a passageway joining the middle ear to the nasopharynx, which allows equalization of pressure — why swallowing relieves ear pressure on descent.

options.t: Carries vibration to the cochlea
options.why: The ossicles carry vibration to the cochlea.

options.t: Drains inner ear fluid to the throat
options.why: It equalizes pressure rather than draining the inner ear.

options.t: Joins middle ear to nasopharynx
Separates ear canal from middle ear
options.why: The tympanic membrane does that.

questions.stem: What separates the ear canal from the middle ear, and what conducts sound to it?
questions.why: The external ear conducts sound to the tympanic membrane (eardrum), which separates the ear canal from the middle ear. The pinna protects the outside ear and collects sound into the canal.

options.t: The oval window
options.why: That lies deeper, between middle and inner ear.

options.t: The eustachian tube
options.why: That connects the middle ear to the throat.

options.t: The tympanic membrane
The cochlear duct
options.why: That is inside the cochlea.

questions.stem: Match each type of pain to its description.
questions.why: Somatic is sharp and locatable; visceral is deep and vague. Referred and phantom are both mismatches between where it hurts and where the problem is.
pairs: Deep pain internally, enclosed within a cavity such as chest or abdomen
In superficial tissues; more intense and more precisely localized
Perceived in a part of the body other than its true source
Sensation of pain in a body part that is no longer present

questions.stem: Match each receptor type to what it detects.
questions.why: Six receptor families. Pain and temperature share a receptor type; the last three are the ones that feed autonomic reflexes rather than conscious sensation.
pairs: Stimuli that could damage the body
Changes in physical properties — touch and pressure
Position in space, from joints, muscles, and tendons
Chemicals in the body or bloodstream

questions.stem: Match each special sense to a defining detail.
questions.why: Smell and taste are both chemical senses requiring the stimulus to dissolve first. Sight and hearing both convert physical energy into neural code.
pairs: Receptors in the upper nasal cavity respond to chemicals dissolved in mucus
Responds to four primary sensations: sweet, salty, sour, bitter
The retina converts the optical image into a neural code
External and middle ear serve hearing only; inner ear adds balance
